Modeling and Process Simulation The process configuration and design basis for a 3,123 tonne/year CO₂ DAC system is described below. It outlines the DAC process and plant layout. Figure 10 illustrates the block flow diagram for the proposed DAC plant, while Figure 11 provides a breakdown of the process flow diagram steps for one DAC cycle. The DAC system begins with adsorption blowers that deliver ambient air to sorbent mats. A mat is defined as an array of beds operating under identical conditions; in this system, there are 5 mats, each comprising 15 beds. The air blowers simultaneously supply two mats for a duration of one hour during the adsorption phase. The time for adsorption was selected as an optimum value achieving higher CO capture efficiency based 2 on experimental results and simulation results using Aspen Adsorption. 14 Figure 10. Full DAC schematic diagram for the proposed DAC plant. Upon completion of adsorption, the respective mat is sealed, and thermal regeneration is initiated by heating the sorbent to 100°C. Concurrently, a vacuum is applied to facilitate desorption of CO₂ and co-adsorbed water. The vacuum step is performed on one mat at a time, with each desorption cycle requiring approximately 30 min. Consequently, two mats are desorbed per hour. The vacuum level and period were also selected based on experimental results and an optimization study done using Aspen Adsorption software. Since water constitutes a significant fraction of the desorbed stream, a primary condenser is positioned upstream of the vacuum pump to condense the bulk of the water vapor. This step improves pump efficiency and mitigates the risk of pump water overloading. Residual water vapor exiting the vacuum pump is removed via a secondary condenser located downstream. The resulting 15 CO₂-rich stream is subsequently compressed to the desired outlet pressure for downstream utilization or storage. Capacity of equipment is estimated using Aspen Plus flowsheet. Following desorption, a cooling air blower directs ambient air through the regenerated mats for 30 min, reducing their temperature to prepare them for the next adsorption cycle. Simultaneously with the desorption step, the desorbed water and carbon dioxide are redirected toward a neighboring mat, serving as a preheating step to recover and transfer sensible heat. This strategy improves overall energy efficiency by reducing the thermal load during subsequent regeneration. Figure 11 provides a detailed breakdown of the steps and their sequence in a DAC cycle. Each step has a duration of 30 min, resulting in a total cycle time of 2.5 hours. The figure illustrates the initial step for each mat in the system, with subsequent steps following sequentially every 30 min as the mat transitions from one operating mode to the next. An optimization study was conducted using Aspen Adsorption to optimize the time for each step in the DAC cycle. Figure 11. Breakdown of steps for each DAC cycle. 2.6. Techno-Economic Analysis Table
